author: Anthony Orrico
title: Staggering $1.5 trillion Trump claims Dems wanted to give to undocumented immigrants for healthcare - NewsBreak
text:
By Anthony Orrico ,
39 minutes ago President Donald Trump signed into law a short-term funding bill that will end the longest government shutdown in United States history after the Republican president refused for over a month to negotiate with Democrats on extending healthcare subsidies.
Before signing the bill, Trump continued to make false claims that Democrats were demanding health insurance for undocumented immigrants, despite them not being able to purchase healthcare from the ACA marketplace , nor access programs like Medicaid or Medicare.
"They wanted to pay them $1.5 trillion, which would have really hurt our health care businesses and our recipients at levels never seen before. Today, we're sending a clear message that we will never give in to extortion, because that's what it was they tried to extort," Trump said.
READ MORE: MAGA rage at Trump's 'unforgivable betrayal' as he says 'you don't' have talent in US
READ MORE: Trump approval rating on economy drops below Biden's worst following shutdown chaos
Trump continued to lay the blame for the 43-day long shutdown squarely at the feet of Democrats, who were steadfast in not voting for a continuing resolution that did not include an extension of ACA subsidies, until eight moderate Democrats struck a deal with Senator Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD) to reopen the government.
"The Democrats tried to extort our country. In just a moment, I'll sign a bill exactly like we asked Democrats to send us all along many days ago. This cost the country $1.5 trillion, this little excursion that they took us on," Trump said.
Without extensions to the ACA subsidies, Americans who purchase their healthcare through the ACA marketplace will likely see their premiums double, triple or even quadruple in some cases.
House Speaker Mike Johnson lambasted Democrats for the historically long shutdown, saying they used the “American people as leverage in this political game.”
“Voters are going to remember which political party played games with their life,” said House Speaker Mike Johnson.
House lawmakers made their long-awaited return to the nation’s capital this week after nearly eight weeks away, with Republicans using their slight majority to get the bill over the finish line by a vote of 222-209. The Senate has already passed the measure. Trump has called the bill a “very big victory.”
The legislation included buy-in from eight senators who broke ranks with the Democrats after reaching the conclusion that Republicans would not bend on using a government funding bill to extend the health care tax credits. Meanwhile, the shutdown’s toll was growing by the day.
The compromise funds three annual spending bills and extends the rest of the government funding through Jan. 30. Republicans promised to hold a vote by mid-December to extend the health care subsidies, but there is no guarantee of success.
“We had reached a point where I think a number of us believed that the shutdown had been very effective in raising the concern about health care,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.). The promise for a future vote “gives us an opportunity to continue to address that going forward.”
The legislation includes a reversal of the firing of federal workers by the Trump administration since the shutdown began. It also protects federal workers against further layoffs through January and guarantees they are paid once the shutdown is over. The bill for the Agriculture Department means people who rely on key food assistance programs will see those benefits funded without threat of interruption through the rest of the budget year.
Thune had signaled earlier this week, in what amounted to a handshake deal with Democrats, that he would allow a separate vote on extension of the ACA subsidies, but that legislation would likely be dead on arrival in the House if it were to pass the Senate.
The House had not been in legislative session since Sept. 19, when it passed a short-term measure to keep the government open when the new budget year began in October. Johnson sent lawmakers home after that vote and put the onus on the Senate to act, saying House Republicans had done their job.
Johnson said the Democratic opposition to the spending bill was pointless, adding, “It was wrong. It was cruel.”
“They knew it would cause pain and they did it anyway,” Johnson said.
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats would not give up even if the vote did not go their way.
“This fight is not over,” Jeffries said. “We’re just getting started.”
The bill only funds the government through Jan. 31, when another shutdown fight is more than likely, as Democrats may continue to leverage the little power they have to get something out of any future shutdown.
